title: Lakshmana leaves the hut
hookLine: everyone knows the line Lakshmana draws; Valmiki gives him a bow instead
carry: pranam: bow to the god in them
last: REMEMBER GOD AT THE LAST BREATH.

cards: In the version told on television and at bedtime, this is the moment of the line. Lakshmana, forced to leave, takes his arrow and draws a line in the earth around the hut.
Don't cross it, he tells Sita, and nothing can harm you. The image is so familiar it has a name of its own. But open Valmiki's Ramayana here, read the scene line by line, and there is no line.

teach.b: The cry reaches the hut: Ha Sita! Ha Lakshmana! Sita hears Rama's voice in pain, and she's terrified.
Go, she tells Lakshmana. Your brother is calling. Lakshmana doesn't move.
No one in the three worlds can defeat Rama, he says, and Rama told me not to leave you. That voice is a rakshasa's trick. And Sita, frightened out of her mind, says terrible things.
You want him dead. You followed us here because you want me. Or you're working for Bharata.
These are words of fear, and the text doesn't pretend otherwise. Lakshmana is shattered. Your words are like red-hot iron arrows in my ears, he says.

teach.h: YOU ARE LIKE A GODDESS TO ME.
teach.b: You are like a goddess to me; I can't answer you. He asks the spirits of the forest to be his witnesses and to protect her. Then he bows to her and goes, looking back again and again.
No line in the dust. A bow.
Much later, shown jewelry Sita dropped from the sky, Lakshmana will say: I don't know her earrings or her armlets, but I know her anklets, because I bowed at her feet every day.

teach.h: PRANAM: BOW TO THE GOD IN THEM.
teach.b: That's pranam, an everyday act in a Hindu home: folding the hands, touching an elder's feet. Many Hindus explain it as honoring something holy in the person in front of you. It isn't agreeing with every word.
Lakshmana tells Sita plainly she's wrong. But he bows to who she is, under the fear.

how: Reciters of Valmiki's Ramayana explain Sita's harsh words to Lakshmana as words of terror for Rama. Pranam, folding the hands or touching an elder's feet (charan sparsh), is an everyday Hindu gesture of respect, and Lakshmana's 'I know her anklets' is often recalled as its model.

o: a vow Sita makes never to leave the hut alone
a boundary Rama draws around the hut before the hunt
a well-known scene Valmiki's telling doesn't have

games.q: at the hut — tap the pairs.
p: known from bowing at her feet

s: in Valmiki, Lakshmana draws a line around the hut
there is no line in Valmiki; he calls on the forest spirits, bows, and goes.
Lakshmana believes the cry is a trick
he's sure no one can defeat Rama.
pranam means agreeing with everything an elder says
it honors who they are. Lakshmana tells Sita she is wrong and still bows.

games.q: your aunt snaps at you at a family puja because she's stressed about the food. after the aarti, everyone touches the elders' feet. what fits Lakshmana's way?
o: touch her feet too: honor who she is, and talk about the snap later if it matters.
skip her; pranam is only for people who've earned it today.
touch her feet and decide her words were right, since elders are always right.
games.why: Lakshmana answered fear with reverence and still told Sita plainly she was wrong. pranam honors the person, not every word.

practice: Try a pranam, the way many Hindus do each morning. Fold your hands at your chest and bow your head. Bring to mind an elder, or someone who's been sharp with you lately because they were scared.
Bow to what's holy in them, not to the harsh words. If you don't pray, simply fold your hands and wish them well. Stay there for a few slow breaths.

wordCard.voice: The line. In Valmiki, Lakshmana draws no line. Cut by Sita's frightened words, he leaves her in the care of the forest spirits, and bows before he goes.

orig.note: Sanskrit vanadevatā: the deities or spirits of the forest, whom Lakshmana calls on to guard Sita.

carryVoice: Today's line: pranam, bow to the god in them. Tomorrow, where the line came from. That's day five hundred seventy.
